title: How Rollercoasters Work, Minus the Fun
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain how roller coasters work, starting with their origins in sixteenth-century Russian ice slides and the French wheeled coaster (Russian Mountains, 1817), then covering early American incline railways, the Great Depression slowdown, and the components of a coaster: chain lifts, linear induction motors, launch systems, and disc-style brakes. They compare wooden and steel track, describe suspended, inverted, flying, stand-up, and four-dimension coasters, and explain the physics of gravity, acceleration, potential and kinetic energy, weightlessness, and airtime. They discuss ride safety statistics from Tom Harris's HowStuffWorks article, a fatal 2011 Chicago incident involving a three-year-old, and records such as the tallest, fastest, and oldest coasters. The episode ends with listener mail about the crowdsourced Japan earthquake e-book "Two Minutes and Forty Six Seconds," with proceeds going to the Japan Red Cross.
topics: Two Minutes and Forty Six Seconds

entities.name: Two Minutes and Forty Six Seconds

segments.title: Opening banter about roller coaster fears and experiences
segments.summary: The hosts trade personal stories about childhood roller coaster fears, Space Mountain, Cedar Point, and Six Flags, and set up the topic.

segments.title: History of roller coasters
segments.summary: Origins in sixteenth-century Russian ice slides, the French move to wheeled coasters with the Russian Mountains in 1817, the mid-1800s Pennsylvania Mauch Chunk railway, early amusement parks, and the slowdown during the Great Depression and World War Two.

segments.title: Lift systems and braking
segments.summary: Components that move the train: chain lifts with chain dogs, catapult launches using linear induction motors or spinning wheels, and disc-style brakes that clamp metal fins, with computer control.

segments.title: Wooden versus steel track
segments.summary: Wooden coasters are limited by stiff planks and high maintenance, and are less precise; steel track allows inversions. Steel tubular track debuted in the 1950s with polyurethane or nylon wheels. Son of the Beast is noted as the tallest wooden coaster.

segments.title: Coaster car types
segments.summary: Suspended, inverted, flying, pipeline, stand-up, and bobsled-style coasters, and how the fourth-dimension design spins seats around the track.

segments.title: Physics of the ride: energy, gravity, acceleration, and sensations
segments.summary: Energy conversion between potential and kinetic energy on hills, Newton's first law, atmospheric weight and the sensation of gravity, opposing feelings from acceleration, weightlessness and airtime, and how organs react differently, plus visual cues and the body not feeling constant velocity.

segments.title: Safety statistics and records
segments.summary: Injury statistics from Tom Harris's article, the Brain Injury Institute study on pre-existing conditions, the recent Go Bananas death of a three-year-old in Chicago, and records for tallest, fastest, steepest, largest woodie, and oldest coasters.

segments.title: Listener mail: Japan earthquake e-book
segments.summary: Listener Jason Jenkins describes the crowdsourced e-book Two Minutes and Forty Six Seconds, with proceeds going to the Japan Red Cross.
